subject: Computer Science
summary: How algorithms are represented (pseudocode, flowcharts) and analysed (asymptotic notation, loop counting, recurrences, Master theorem), the main design paradigms (divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming) and the standard graph algorithms (BFS, DFS, MST, shortest paths). DSSSB regularly asks complexity values, flowchart symbols and short traces of these algorithms.

sections.heading: Algorithm: definition, characteristics and pseudocode
sections.body:
An **algorithm** is a finite sequence of well-defined steps that solves a problem. It is independent of any programming language; a **program** is its implementation in a particular language.
Characteristics (Knuth):
- **Input**: zero or more quantities are supplied.
- **Output**: at least one quantity is produced.
- **Definiteness**: every step is clear and unambiguous.
- **Finiteness**: it terminates after a finite number of steps.
- **Effectiveness**: every step is basic enough to be carried out exactly, in finite time.
Ways to express an algorithm: natural language, **flowchart** (graphical) and **pseudocode** (structured English close to code, with no strict syntax).
Common pseudocode conventions: `BEGIN ... END`, `READ`/`INPUT`, `PRINT`/`OUTPUT`, assignment with `←` or `=`, `IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF`, `WHILE ... ENDWHILE`, `FOR i ← 1 TO n ... ENDFOR`. Pseudocode is easy to convert into any language and easy to modify; flowcharts show the logic visually but become clumsy for large programs.

code.source:
ALGORITHM LargestOfN
BEGIN
    READ n, A[1..n]
    max ← A[1]
    FOR i ← 2 TO n DO
        IF A[i] > max THEN
            max ← A[i]
        ENDIF
    ENDFOR
    PRINT max
END

sections.heading: Flowcharts and the three basic constructs
sections.body:
A **flowchart** is a diagram of an algorithm using standard (ANSI/ISO) symbols joined by **flow lines** (arrows). Flow is normally top to bottom and left to right; there is one Start and at least one Stop, and a decision box has one entry and two (or more) labelled exits.
**Structured programming** (Böhm–Jacopini theorem): any algorithm can be built from three control structures:
- **Sequence**: steps one after another.
- **Selection (decision)**: choose a path with a condition (if-else, case). Drawn with a **diamond**.
- **Iteration (loop/repetition)**: repeat while a condition holds; in a flowchart, a flow line goes back to an earlier decision.

sections.heading: Measuring efficiency: asymptotic notations
sections.body:
The efficiency of an algorithm is measured by its **time complexity** (number of basic operations) and **space complexity** (memory), as functions of input size n. **A priori** analysis is done on the algorithm before implementation; **a posteriori** analysis measures the running program. Analyses consider the **best**, **average** and **worst** case (e.g. linear search: 1, about n/2 and n comparisons).
Asymptotic notations describe growth for large n, ignoring constants and lower-order terms:
- **Big-O, f(n) = O(g(n))**: there exist c > 0 and n₀ such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. **Upper bound.**
- **Big-Omega, Ω(g(n))**: f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. **Lower bound.**
- **Theta, Θ(g(n))**: c₁·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂·g(n). **Tight bound** (both O and Ω).
- **Little-o** and **little-omega**: strict upper and lower bounds (f/g → 0 and f/g → ∞).
Rules: keep the dominant term and drop constants: 3n² + 10n log n + 7 = Θ(n²). A polynomial of degree k is Θ(nᵏ). Log bases differ only by a constant, so O(log₂n) = O(log₁₀n). But 2²ⁿ is not O(2ⁿ).
Order of growth: **1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ**.

sections.heading: Counting loops and solving recurrences
sections.body:
**Loops**: count how many times the innermost statement runs.
- `for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)` → n times: O(n).
- `for (i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2)` → ⌊log₂n⌋ + 1 times: O(log n). The same holds for `i = i / 2` going down from n.
- Two nested loops of n each → n²; inner loop `j = 1..i` → n(n + 1)/2: still O(n²).
- `for (i = 1; i * i <= n; i++)` → ⌊√n⌋ times: O(√n).
- Consecutive loops add; nested loops multiply.
**Recurrences** describe recursive algorithms. They are solved by substitution, the recursion-tree method or the **Master theorem**.
**Master theorem** for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), a ≥ 1, b > 1. Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a):
- Case 1: f(n) polynomially smaller → T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)).
- Case 2: f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)) → T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n).
- Case 3: f(n) polynomially larger (and a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) for some c < 1) → T(n) = Θ(f(n)).
It does not apply to "subtract" recurrences like T(n) = T(n - 1) + n; expand those directly.

sections.heading: Complexity classes: P, NP, NP-complete, NP-hard
sections.body:
- **P**: decision problems solvable in **polynomial time** (e.g. sorting, shortest path, MST). These are called tractable.
- **NP**: problems whose proposed solution can be **verified** in polynomial time (equivalently, solvable in polynomial time by a non-deterministic machine). P ⊆ NP; whether **P = NP** is an open problem.
- **NP-hard**: at least as hard as every problem in NP (every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time); it need not be in NP.
- **NP-complete**: in NP **and** NP-hard. **SAT** was the first problem proved NP-complete (**Cook's theorem**). Others: 3-SAT, vertex cover, clique, Hamiltonian cycle, graph colouring, subset sum, decision versions of TSP and 0/1 knapsack.
The O(nW) dynamic-programming solution of 0/1 knapsack is **pseudo-polynomial**: polynomial in the value of W, not in the number of bits needed to write it. The **halting problem** is undecidable: no algorithm can solve it at all.

sections.heading: Divide and conquer
sections.body:
**Divide and conquer** solves a problem in three steps: **divide** it into smaller sub-problems of the same type, **conquer** them recursively (solving small cases directly) and **combine** their solutions. The sub-problems are independent; if they overlap, dynamic programming is better.
- **Binary search**: one half is searched: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 = O(log n).
- **Merge sort**: split into halves, sort each, merge in O(n): Θ(n log n) in all cases. Merging two sorted lists of sizes m and n needs at most m + n - 1 comparisons.
- **Quick sort**: **partition** around a pivot (smaller elements to the left, larger to the right), then sort both parts; the work is in dividing, and combining is trivial. Best/average O(n log n); worst O(n²) when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element. A randomised or median-of-three pivot makes the worst case unlikely.
- **Max-min**: about 3n/2 - 2 comparisons (n a power of 2) instead of 2n - 2.
- **Strassen's matrix multiplication**: 7 multiplications of n/2 × n/2 matrices instead of 8 → O(n^2.81). **Karatsuba** integer multiplication: O(n^1.585).

code.source:
def merge_sort(a, depth=0):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left = merge_sort(a[:mid], depth + 1)
    right = merge_sort(a[mid:], depth + 1)
    merged, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:          # <= keeps the sort stable
            merged.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(right[j]); j += 1
    merged += left[i:] + right[j:]
    print("  " * depth + "merge", left, right, "->", merged)
    return merged

sections.heading: Greedy method
sections.body:
A **greedy algorithm** builds a solution step by step, always taking the choice that looks best **at that moment**, and never reconsiders it. It gives an optimal answer only when the problem has:
- the **greedy-choice property**: a locally optimal choice is part of some globally optimal solution, and
- **optimal substructure**: an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to sub-problems.
Classic greedy algorithms:
- **Fractional knapsack**: sort items by value/weight ratio, take the best ratios first, the last one partly: O(n log n).
- **Activity selection**: sort by **finish time**, pick each activity that starts after the last chosen one ends.
- **Huffman coding**: repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency nodes; gives an optimal **prefix code**: O(n log n).
- **Job sequencing with deadlines**, **Kruskal's** and **Prim's** MST, **Dijkstra's** shortest paths.
Greedy **fails** for **0/1 knapsack** (items cannot be split) and for coin change with arbitrary denominations: with coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6, greedy gives 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) but 3 + 3 (2 coins) is optimal.

code.source:
def fractional_knapsack(items, W):
    # items: (name, value, weight); best value/weight ratio first
    items = sorted(items, key=lambda t: t[1] / t[2], reverse=True)
    total = 0
    for name, v, w in items:
        if W == 0:
            break
        take = min(w, W)
        total += v * take / w
        W -= take
        print(f"take {take}/{w} of {name}")
    return total

items = [("I1", 40, 5), ("I2", 36, 6), ("I3", 45, 9), ("I4", 20, 10)]
print("value =", fractional_knapsack(items, 15))

sections.heading: Dynamic programming
sections.body:
**Dynamic programming (DP)** solves problems with **overlapping sub-problems** and **optimal substructure** by solving each sub-problem **once** and storing its answer (Bellman's principle of optimality).
- **Memoization (top-down)**: write the natural recursion and cache results.
- **Tabulation (bottom-up)**: fill a table from the smallest sub-problems upwards.
Naive recursive Fibonacci takes exponential time because the same calls repeat; DP makes it O(n).
Standard DP problems: **0/1 knapsack** O(nW), **longest common subsequence** O(mn), **matrix-chain multiplication** O(n³), **Floyd–Warshall** all-pairs shortest paths O(V³), **Bellman–Ford** O(VE), optimal BST, edit distance, multistage graphs, coin change (minimum coins), and TSP in O(n²·2ⁿ).
LCS recurrence: if xᵢ = yⱼ then L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1, else L[i][j] = max(L[i-1][j], L[i][j-1]).
Multiplying a p × q matrix by a q × r matrix costs **p·q·r** scalar multiplications; matrix-chain DP chooses the bracketing that minimises the total.

sections.heading: Graph traversal: BFS, DFS and topological sort
sections.body:
**Breadth-first search (BFS)** visits the start vertex, then all its neighbours, then their neighbours (level by level) using a **queue**. In an unweighted graph it finds the **shortest path in number of edges**. It is also used for level-order traversal and bipartite testing.
**Depth-first search (DFS)** goes as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a **stack** or recursion. Uses: cycle detection, **topological sort**, connected and strongly connected components, path finding, maze solving.
Both take **O(V + E)** with adjacency lists and **O(V²)** with an adjacency matrix. The exact visiting order depends on the order in which neighbours are listed; exam questions usually assume ascending or alphabetical order.
**Topological sort** orders the vertices of a **DAG** so that every edge u → v has u before v. Methods: reverse of DFS finishing order, or **Kahn's algorithm** (repeatedly remove a vertex with in-degree 0). A graph with a cycle has no topological order. A DAG may have several valid orders.

sections.heading: Minimum spanning trees: Kruskal and Prim
sections.body:
A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** of a connected, undirected, weighted graph connects all V vertices with **V - 1 edges** and the least total weight. If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is **unique**. Both algorithms below are **greedy**.
**Kruskal's algorithm**: sort all edges by weight; add the next lightest edge if it does **not form a cycle** (checked with a disjoint-set/union-find structure); stop after V - 1 edges. The partial solution is a **forest**. Time **O(E log E)** = O(E log V), dominated by sorting.
**Prim's algorithm**: start from any vertex and repeatedly add the **lightest edge connecting the tree to a new vertex**. The partial solution is always **one tree**. Time **O(V²)** with an adjacency matrix (good for dense graphs) or **O(E log V)** with a binary heap.
Kruskal suits sparse graphs; Prim with a matrix suits dense graphs. Both give the same total weight, though they may pick different trees when weights tie.

sections.heading: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman–Ford, Floyd–Warshall
sections.body:
**Relaxation** of edge (u, v) with weight w: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] = dist[u] + w.
- **Dijkstra** (single source, greedy): repeatedly finalise the unvisited vertex with the smallest distance and relax its edges. Requires **non-negative** edge weights. Time **O(V²)** with an array (the textbook answer), **O((V + E) log V)** with a binary heap.
- **Bellman–Ford** (single source, DP): relax all edges **V - 1 times**; works with **negative edges** and **detects negative-weight cycles** (if a V-th pass still relaxes an edge). Time **O(VE)**.
- **Floyd–Warshall** (all pairs, DP): for each intermediate vertex k, dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). Time **O(V³)**, space O(V²); negative edges allowed but no negative cycles.
- Unweighted graph: plain **BFS** gives shortest paths in O(V + E).

formulas.name: Big-O definition
formulas.formula: f(n) = O(g(n)) ⇔ ∃ c > 0, n₀ : 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
formulas.note: Ω reverses the inequality; Θ means both hold.

formulas.name: Master theorem
formulas.formula: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) with n^(log_b a)
formulas.note: Smaller → Θ(n^(log_b a)); equal → Θ(n^(log_b a) log n); larger (with regularity) → Θ(f(n)).

formulas.name: Doubling loop
formulas.formula: for (i = 1; i ≤ n; i *= 2) runs ⌊log₂n⌋ + 1 times
formulas.note: The loop test is evaluated one extra time (when it fails).

formulas.name: Arithmetic series
formulas.note: Nested loop with inner bound i → O(n²).

formulas.name: Geometric series
formulas.note: Gives the Tower of Hanoi count 2ⁿ - 1 moves.

formulas.name: Matrix multiplication cost
formulas.formula: (p × q)·(q × r) costs p·q·r scalar multiplications

formulas.name: Relaxation
formulas.formula: if d[u] + w(u, v) < d[v] then d[v] ← d[u] + w(u, v)
formulas.note: Core step of Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford.

(a) a = 4, b = 2: n^(log₂4) = n². f(n) = n is polynomially smaller → Case 1 → **Θ(n²)**
(b) a = 2, b = 2: n^(log₂2) = n = f(n) → Case 2 → **Θ(n log n)**
(c) a = 3, b = 4: n^(log₄3) ≈ n^0.79. f(n) = n² is larger; regularity: 3(n/4)² = (3/16)n² ≤ c·n² with c = 3/16 < 1 → Case 3 → **Θ(n²)**
(d) a = 1, b = 2: n^(log₂1) = n⁰ = 1 = f(n) → Case 2 → **Θ(log n)**

workedExamples.problem: Knapsack capacity 15. Items (value, weight): I1 (40, 5), I2 (36, 6), I3 (45, 9), I4 (20, 10). Find the optimal value (a) if items can be split (fractional) and (b) if each item is taken whole or not at all (0/1). Does greedy-by-ratio solve (b)?
workedExamples.solution:
Ratios: I1 = 8, I2 = 6, I3 = 5, I4 = 2.
(a) Greedy by ratio: I1 (weight 5, value 40) → I2 (weight 11, value 76) → 4 units of I3 = 4/9 × 45 = 20 → full. Value = **96**.
(b) Greedy by ratio picks I1 and I2 (weight 11, value 76); I3 (9) and I4 (10) no longer fit → 76.
Check all feasible pairs: I1 + I3 = weight 14, value **85**; I2 + I3 = 15, 81; I1 + I4 = 15, 60. No three items fit (smallest three weigh 20).
Optimal 0/1 value = **85**, so greedy fails for 0/1 knapsack; use DP.

workedExamples.problem: Matrices A1 (10 × 20), A2 (20 × 5), A3 (5 × 30). Find the minimum number of scalar multiplications to compute A1·A2·A3.
workedExamples.solution:
Two bracketings are possible:
- (A1·A2)·A3: A1·A2 costs 10 × 20 × 5 = 1000 and gives 10 × 5; then (10 × 5)·(5 × 30) costs 10 × 5 × 30 = 1500. Total = **2500**.
- A1·(A2·A3): A2·A3 costs 20 × 5 × 30 = 3000 and gives 20 × 30; then (10 × 20)·(20 × 30) costs 10 × 20 × 30 = 6000. Total = 9000.
Minimum = **2500** with (A1·A2)·A3.

workedExamples.problem: Undirected graph edges: A–B 4, A–C 3, B–C 1, B–D 2, C–D 4, C–E 6, D–E 5. Find the MST using Kruskal's algorithm and check it with Prim's algorithm starting at A.
workedExamples.solution:
Kruskal: sorted edges: B–C 1, B–D 2, A–C 3, A–B 4, C–D 4, D–E 5, C–E 6.
- B–C 1 → take
- B–D 2 → take
- A–C 3 → take
- A–B 4 → A and B already connected (A–C–B): reject (cycle)
- C–D 4 → reject (C–B–D)
- D–E 5 → take. Now 4 = V - 1 edges: stop.
MST = {B–C, B–D, A–C, D–E}, weight 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = **11**.
Prim from A: lightest edge from {A} is A–C 3; from {A, C}: C–B 1; from {A, B, C}: B–D 2; from {A, B, C, D}: D–E 5 (cheaper than C–E 6). Same tree, weight **11**.

workedExamples.problem: The Tower of Hanoi recursion moves n - 1 discs, then the largest disc, then n - 1 discs again: T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + 1, T(1) = 1. Solve it and find the moves for 5 discs.

pitfalls: Big-O is only an upper bound: an O(n²) algorithm is also O(n³). Θ gives the exact growth rate.
The Master theorem does not apply to T(n) = T(n - 1) + n; expanding it gives Θ(n²).
Dijkstra's algorithm can give wrong answers with negative edge weights; use Bellman–Ford.
Greedy works for fractional knapsack but not for 0/1 knapsack.
Quick sort is divide and conquer, but its worst case is O(n²), not O(n log n).
Topological sort exists only for directed acyclic graphs, and the order need not be unique.
Kruskal builds a forest that becomes a tree at the end; Prim always keeps a single tree.
An MST has V - 1 edges; a graph with V vertices and fewer than V - 1 edges cannot be connected.
In a flowchart, input/output is a parallelogram and processing is a rectangle; the diamond is only for decisions.
An algorithm must terminate (finiteness) and needs at least one output, but it may have zero inputs.
quickRevision: Algorithm characteristics: input (≥ 0), output (≥ 1), definiteness, finiteness, effectiveness.
Efficiency is measured in time and space.
O = upper bound, Ω = lower bound, Θ = tight bound.
Growth: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ.
Halving or doubling loops are O(log n); nested n × n loops are O(n²).
Binary search T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 = O(log n); merge sort T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = O(n log n).
Greedy: fractional knapsack, activity selection, Huffman, Prim, Kruskal, Dijkstra.
DP: 0/1 knapsack O(nW), LCS O(mn), matrix chain O(n³), Floyd–Warshall O(V³), Bellman–Ford O(VE).
DP = overlapping sub-problems + optimal substructure; memoization is top-down, tabulation bottom-up.
BFS uses a queue, DFS a stack; both O(V + E) with adjacency lists.
Dijkstra: O(V²) with arrays, O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap; no negative edges.
Kruskal O(E log E); Prim O(V²) or O(E log V).
Flowchart: oval = start/stop, rectangle = process, parallelogram = I/O, diamond = decision, circle = connector.
SAT was the first NP-complete problem (Cook's theorem).
